species.diagnosis: Large pelobatoid anuran. Cranial roof wide and short; presacral vertebrae procoelous; sacral diapophysis strongly expanded; possesses typical fossorial skeletal features: robust spade-like prehallux; tibiofibula shorter than femur; calcaneus and astragalus short. Distinguished from Pelobatidae by: paired frontoparietals (triradiate in Pelobates and Eopelobates); calcaneus and astragalus not fused; sacrum-urostyle joint single-condylar.
species.remarks: Originally named Bufo linquensis by Yang (1977). Gao (1986) established M. cratus based on the same material, but this is a junior synonym. Roczek et al. (2011) corrected the nomenclatural history and designated IVPP V 7700 as neotype. The species shows adaptation for fossorial habits, being the earliest known fossorial anuran.

species.diagnosis: Large toad species; skull short and broadly rounded; parasphenoid cultriform process width less than half its length, lateral wings perpendicular to long axis; anterior margin of sacral diapophysis perpendicular to body axis, posterior margin slightly inclined, thus diapophysis slightly expanded; sacrum-urostyle joint bicondylar; tibiofibula shorter than femur.
species.remarks: Represents the oldest preserved skeleton of a bufonid in the Northern Hemisphere. Reappeared in Eurasia after a large temporal gap between the Paleocene and early Miocene (Rage, 2003; Rage et Roczek, 2003). The holotype (SDM) JMSP H11-038 was originally designated as paratype of Bufo linquensis by Yang (1977).

species.diagnosis: Small Rana species (snout-vent length 29-46 mm); skull tapering anteriorly forming triangular shape; frontoparietals smooth, with markedly thickened area ventrally; posterior presacral transverse processes perpendicular to body midline; urostyle bicondylar with sacrum; ilium with prominent dorsal ridge; tibiofibula significantly longer than femur (femur:tibiofibula = 0.71-0.90), indicating strong jumping ability.
species.remarks: Holotype was lost. Young (1936) did not designate a holotype or provide specimen numbers. Roczek et al. (2011) designated a neotype (IVPP V 11706) and a paratype (IVPP V 14264), but the paratype designation is invalid under ICZN rules. Sanchiz (1998) considered this a nomen dubium. Questionable species, hence '?' added to species name.

species.diagnosis: Head triangular, width slightly greater than length; maxilla straight, snout relatively pointed; frontoparietals relatively wide, trapezoidal, slightly wider posteriorly; orbit elliptical, anterior end slightly narrower than posterior; vertebrae wider than long; second presacral transverse process distally inclined anteriorly; hindlimbs slender, tibiofibula slightly longer than femur; phalangeal tips not expanded.
species.remarks: Liu (1961) considered this species most similar to R. nigromaculata, distinguished by head width greater than length, wider frontoparietals, and similar transverse process dimensions. species.diagnosis: Compared with other species of Liaobatrachus, L. zhaoi has relatively longer hindlimbs, femur and tibiofibula subequal in length, maxilla without palatine process, parasphenoid cultriform process gradually narrowing from 1/2 point anteriorly, acetabulum semicircular, pubis ossified in fully developed adults.

species.remarks: Remark This species was established by Gao and Shubin (2003) based on four specimens from Daohugou, Inner Mongolia. Species name derived from the ancient name 'Tianyi' of Ningcheng County; holotype total length approximately 160 mm, plus three referred specimens. However, according to ICZN Article 72.4.5, the three other specimens published in the same paper (PKU PV 0210- 0212) should also belong to the type series, and specimens in the type series other than the holotype should be designated as paratypes. Therefore, this book changes these three specimens from referred specimens as originally designated to paratypes.

species.remarks:
Remark Phylogenetic analysis shows Regalerpeton and Chunerpeton form successive sister groups of extant Cryptobranchidae (Zhang et al., 2009), and this genus's vomerine tooth row morphology, pterygoid, and other typical features are all consistent with Cryptobranchidae, so this book assigns this genus to Cryptobranchidae. The genus name derives from its fossil locality Weichang, Hebei, once a royal hunting ground during the Qing Dynasty.
Remark Species name from fossil locality Weichang. This species' scapulocoracoid morphology is quite special, very similar to hynobiids like Liaoxitriton, but quite different from Chunerpeton, which also belongs to Cryptobranchidae.

species.remarks: Remark Liaoxitriton was established by Dong Zhiming and Wang Yuan (1998) based on 34 specimens from Huludao, Liaoning, named after its location in western Liaoning; over the following decade, hundreds more specimens were found at this locality. These specimens' locality was once mistakenly identified as 'Shajiaocheng, Huludao' (Dong Zhiming, Wang Yuan, 1998). Wang (2001) revised the locality to 'Wangbao, Huludao' (likely a misspelling of 'Wangbaoshan, Huludao'). Wang Yuan (2002), based on field surveys, finally identified the locality as 'Shuikouzi Village, Wangbaoshan Brigade, Xintaimen Town, Huludao.' Regarding the fossil horizon correlation, different opinions exist. Dong Zhiming and Wang Yuan (1998) considered it the Lower Cretaceous Jiufotang Formation; Wang Yuan (2002), based on amygdaloidal basalt exposures in the region, considered the Yixian Formation possibility cannot be excluded. Wang Sien identified conchostracan specimens collected by Wang Yuan from the same Liaoxitriton horizon as Eosestheria sp. and Eosestheria cf. middendorfii, correlating the strata to the Yixian Formation or basal Jiufotang Formation. Zhang Lijun et al. (2004) reported a second Liaoxitriton-bearing horizon in this area, with Ephemeropsis trisetalis, Eosestheria ovata, Liaoningogladus boii, Sphenaron sp., Ephedrites? sp., etc., and based on the co-occurrence of Eosestheria ovata and Liaoningogladus boii, concluded the horizon should be Yixian Formation, not Jiufotang Formation. species.remarks:
Remark Sinerpeton and Laccotriton come from the same locality, same horizon, and same fossil excavation pit, with many skeletal features similar. Whether this genus is a synonym of the latter is worth exploring. See remarks on the species below.
Remark All specimens of this genus and species come from the same locality and horizon as Laccotriton subsolanus, but Gao and Shubin (2001) considered Sinerpeton fengshanensis as a paedomorphic form, distinguishing it from metamorphosed Laccotriton subsolanus. However, Wang (2006) pointed out Sinerpeton's slender ceratobranchial cannot support external gills; this ceratobranchial is likely the first pair, common in metamorphosed urodels, so whether Sinerpeton is paedomorphic remains questionable. Additionally, S. fengshanensis holotype is very similar to Liaoxitriton zhongjiani juvenile skeletal features, so whether the former is a junior synonym of the latter requires further research. Accordingly, Wang et al. (2008) added a question mark '?' to Sinerpeton. This book also tentatively adopts this approach.

species.diagnosis:
Diagnostic features Small body, slender weak limbs; tail length less than half total length; body may have uniformly fine tubercular spots, but no large dorsolateral or lateral spots. Head size and shape very similar to Cynops orientalis, but body length approximately one-quarter to one-third smaller, the smallest known Cynops species (Yang Zhongjian, 1965).
Estes (1981) provided a completely different set of diagnostic features, but apparently more effective: distinguished from extant Cynops species by nares more dorsally positioned (if specimen not deformed), lacking sagittal tubercle, and body length smaller than extant species. Additionally, Estes (1981) noted this genus is clearly closely related to Cynops, but at higher latitude habitat (400 km north of Cynops orientalis).
Diagnostic features same as genus.
Remark Yang Zhongjian (1965) provided original data showing the holotype has preserved length 43.3 mm, two paratypes 47 mm and 48 mm, estimated total length 47-49 mm, thus smaller than Cynops orientalis; also described as 'skull outline a fairly clear pentagon,' 'nares with slight distance from anterior margin, not as close to anterior edge as modern species,' 'skin impressions also different... dorsal ridge structure not observed.' Because the naming author did not provide other sufficient diagnostic features, whether this genus is valid remains questionable.
Diagnostic features Usually with distinct dorsal crest.

species.diagnosis: Diagnostic features A Late Jurassic paedomorphic Salamandroidea member, with the following unique character combination: skull broader than long, with anterodorsal fenestra and anteromedial fenestra; premaxilla and maxilla outer surfaces with sensory grooves; prefrontal and lacrimal present; palatine separate and dentate; marginal teeth nonpedicellate, simple钉-shaped and significantly shorter than vomerine teeth; parasphenoid posterolateral wings with groove for internal carotid artery; operculum separate from columella; first and second hypobranchials ossified; first and second basibranchials fused; angular lost, fused with prearticular; 15 presacral vertebrae; vertebrae shortened, strongly constricted, with distinct subcentral keel; digital formula 2-2-3-2/3, pedal formula 2-2-3-4-3.
species.remarks:
Remark Near completion of this book, Gao Keqin and Shubin named Beiyanerpeton, a new genus assigned to Salamandroidea incertae familiae. The genus name derives from 'Beiyan,' the name of the fossil locality during China's 'Sixteen Kingdoms' period. Gao and Shubin (2012), through phylogenetic analysis, considered Beiyanerpeton the most basal member of Salamandroidea, and inferred that the divergence of the two major urodelan suborders (Cryptobranchia and Salamandroidea) predates the Late Jurassic (possibly Middle Jurassic), with divergence occurring on Eurasia.
Remark Gao and Shubin (2012) established B. jianpingensis based on 6 numbered specimens (PKU PV 0601-0606) and several unnumbered specimens; species name from fossil locality Jianping County. species.diagnosis:
Jeholotriton differs significantly from Chunerpeton and Liaoxitriton from the same locality in osteological features, distinguishable by pterygoid, vomerine tooth row, external gill, scapulocoracoid morphology, and ossification of carpals, tarsals, and hyoid apparatus. Jeholotriton's pterygoid directed toward skull midline, vomerine tooth row longitudinal, scapulocoracoid coracoid end nearly circular, carpals and tarsals unossified, hyoid ossification very weak. Notably, although Jeholotriton shares with Chunerpeton from the same locality three pairs of feather-like external gills, it differs from Chunerpeton in lacking ossified gill rakers, so even young individuals can be distinguished by this feature.

species.diagnosis:
Diagnostic features Medium-sized individual, skull length over 300 mm; numerous marginal teeth (approximately 45), lower jaw with multiple large caniniform teeth (12), subsequent teeth gradually decreasing anteriorly to posteriorly; lower jaw surface ornamentation honeycomb-type; dentary with dental sulcus parallel to upper margin; coronoid and precoronoid edentulous; Meckelian fenestra large.
Remark Ingentidens named for its large mandibular teeth. The naming authors considered this genus most similar to Chroniosaurus and Chroniosuchus morphologically, but distinguished by larger Meckelian fenestra, edentulous coronoid surface, and teeth 5-16
species.remarks:
Remark Species name from fossil locality 'Hexi Corridor.' This species currently has only one holotype mandible, preserved length approximately 310 mm, representing a relatively large chroniosuchid.
Remark The genus name means 'brother of chroniosuchids.' This genus is clearly smaller than Ingentidens, and its caniniform teeth fewer, teeth pleurodont, size relatively uniform, distinguishing it from Ingentidens at the same locality.
Remark Species name indicates fossil from 'northern slope of Qilian Mountains.' Although specimen preservation is poor, the dorsal margin structure of the maxilla indicates this animal's skull had two preorbital fenestrae. Specimen preserved length approximately 115 mm (including premaxilla and maxilla),

Diagnostic features Small chroniosuchid (maxillary tooth row approximately 115 mm, estimated skull length 170 mm). Distinguished from Russian chroniosuchids by more robust caniniform teeth; distinguished from Ingentidens by distinct pleurodont dentition, fewer caniniform teeth (three on dentary), and more consistent tooth morphology (maxillary teeth similar in shape and size).
Diagnostic features same as genus.

species.diagnosis: Diagnostic features same as genus.
species.remarks: Remark The original paper mentioned approximately 30 specimens [including holotype (XGMRM) XMGM6, IVPP V7391.1- 11 and unnumbered specimens]. According to ICZN Article 72.4.5, referred specimens published in the same paper should also belong to the type series, and specimens other than the holotype should be paratypes. Therefore, this book changes these specimens from referred specimens to paratypes.
